paras: The Greenwood County church burning was the burning of a Black church ("a negro church") in the backwoods of Greenwood County, South Carolina, reported in a single state-news item in April 1903. The same item said that three white men were shot and wounded that night and refused to say how; it named no one responsible for the fire and did not say how the two incidents were connected. A month earlier, three white farmers of the county's Phoenix section had been reported shot from ambush in an attack rumored to have been made by Black men, though none of those reports mentions a church.

The Phoenix section lay in the lower part of Greenwood County, and the March shooting was placed "at some place below Callison, a postoffice about ten miles below" the town of Greenwood. News from that district reached Greenwood slowly, and the correspondent there wrote that "No one from that section seems to know anything about it."

According to the Lexington Dispatch of April 15, 1903, "a negro church was burned and three white men were shot and wounded on the same night in the backwoods of Greenwood county." The brief gave no date, did not name the church or its congregation, and said nothing about who set the fire. Its only other detail was that the wounded men "decline to tell how they got hurt."

The wounded men may have been those named in a Greenwood dispatch of March 19 to The State: Robert G. Cheatham, Robert Quattlebaum and Clebe Penn, "three well known white farmers of the Phoenix section," shot from ambush at 2 o'clock that morning. Cheatham took a charge of buckshot in the hands, arms and chest, Quattlebaum had his left arm broken, and Penn was struck in the left calf with bird shot; Cheatham's physician expected him to recover unless complications set in. The dispatch said it was "reported that the shooting was done by negroes and that seven or eight volleys were exchanged," but added that "those who really know are extremely reticient."

No report states that the church fire and the Phoenix ambush took place on the same night, although the April brief's three wounded white men in the Greenwood backwoods, and their silence, resemble the March accounts. If the two are the same, the church burned on the night of March 18-19, 1903; otherwise the fire can be dated only by its report in mid-April.
No report of an arrest, inquest or official inquiry into either the church burning or the shooting was found.

The shooting of the three farmers travelled widely: an Associated Press version datelined Charleston ran on March 20 in the Savannah Morning News under the headline "Shot From Ambush" and in the Richmond Times Dispatch, and a week later in the Marlboro Democrat. That wire version said "the desperadoes were negroes," a claim it attributed only to report.

The longer State dispatch was reprinted in the Newberry Herald and News, whose headline declared the "Would-be Assassins Supposed to be Negroes," and in the Sumter Watchman and Southron, the Keowee Courier and the Kingstree County Record.

The church burning, by contrast, appeared as one sentence in the Lexington Dispatch, set among state items on a Confederate monument, the end of the Aiken winter season and a post office burglary, with no headline or comment. No account of either the church burning or the shooting was found in the Black press.

bases: The only report describes the burning of a 'negro church' by unnamed persons, with no crowd, attack on residents or expulsion described (A8).
The church burning appears only in one undated sentence in A8; the March shooting reports (A1, A3) corroborate the wounding of three white men in Greenwood County but never mention a church.

accounts.label: South Carolina state-news brief
accounts.gist: A Black church was burned and three white men shot and wounded on the same night in the Greenwood County backwoods; the men would not say how they were hurt.

accounts.label: Greenwood dispatch to The State
accounts.gist: Three white farmers were shot from ambush at 2 a.m. on 19 March; it was 'reported' that Black men did the shooting and that seven or eight volleys were exchanged, but details were meagre and those who knew were silent.

accounts.label: AP wire from Charleston
accounts.gist: The same ambush, with the 'desperadoes' reported to be 'negroes'.

framing.detail: The Lexington Dispatch gave the church burning a single flat sentence among miscellaneous state items, with no headline, motive or comment.
The Newberry Herald and News headlined the March shooting 'Would-be Assassins Supposed to be Negroes', while its text said only that 'it is reported' and that details were 'very meagre'.
The AP version, headed 'Shot From Ambush', called the attackers 'desperadoes' reported to be 'negroes'.
